entities.name: Quintus Sulpicius Longus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Quintus Sulpicius Longus was a Roman patrician who served as one of six consular tribunes in 390 BC, a period marked by the Gaulish conquest of Rome. Born into the gens Sulpicii, a prominent Roman family, Longus played a pivotal role in the tumultuous events leading up to the fall of Rome to the Gauls. His tenure as consular tribune was characterized by the Roman people's increasing discontent with the aristocratic elite, which would eventually contribute to the downfall of the Roman Republic.

The Gaulish invasion, led by Brennus, brought significant destruction to Rome, leaving the city in ruins. Longus's leadership during this period was marked by the Roman Senate's inability to effectively respond to the crisis, further eroding the authority of the patrician class. The consequences of this event would have far-reaching impacts on Roman politics and society, shaping the course of the city's future.

The legacy of Quintus Sulpicius Longus extends beyond his own lifetime, as the events of 390 BC contributed to the rise of the Roman people and the eventual fall of the Roman Republic. His actions, though small in scope, were part of a larger narrative of power struggles and social change that would define the ancient world.

The year 390 BC is etched in history as the point at which Rome's imperial ambitions were checked, and the Roman people asserted their dominance over their government. This moment marked a turning point in the city's development, one that would have lasting effects on the Roman Republic's political and social structures.
